questions.q: In the old network-perimeter model, what typically granted a user broad access to internal systems?
options: A device compliance certificate issued at provisioning
Successfully connecting to the corporate network or VPN, after which little else was checked
A per-request risk score evaluated by Identity Protection
A time-boxed role activation through Privileged Identity Management
questions.explain: Classic perimeter security trusted the network itself: once a user was on the VPN or office network, a username and password were often all that stood between them and a wide range of internal systems.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what specifically broke the assumption that 'the network' and 'the organization' were the same shape?
options: SaaS applications, remote and mobile connectivity, and public cloud resources that sit outside any network you control
The introduction of stronger passwords
Privileged Identity Management replacing standing admin roles
Conditional Access policies becoming mandatory for all tenants
questions.explain: Once resources lived in SaaS apps, public cloud, and were reached by employees on home Wi-Fi or mobile data, the network boundary no longer mapped to the organization's actual footprint.

questions.q: In the zero-trust 'verify explicitly' model, what role does network location play in an access decision?
options: It is the single deciding factor, exactly as in the old model
It is ignored entirely and never evaluated
It is disabled once Conditional Access is configured
It becomes one signal among several — useful, but neither sufficient nor necessary on its own
questions.explain: Zero trust evaluates identity, device, risk, and resource sensitivity on every request; network location is still a usable signal but no longer the thing that decides trust by itself.

questions.q: How does this lesson describe the relationship between Conditional Access / PIM and the 'identity is the new perimeter' idea?
options: Conditional Access and PIM are unrelated legacy tools that zero trust is meant to replace
PIM eliminates the need for Conditional Access entirely
Conditional Access and PIM already treat identity-plus-context as the real control point — this chapter makes that pattern explicit and extends it
Conditional Access only applies to network firewalls, not identity
questions.explain: Conditional Access evaluates identity and context on every sign-in, and PIM treats privileged access as eligible-and-activated rather than standing — both already embody verify-explicitly, which this chapter builds on.

questions.q: The lesson lists three concrete things that change once identity becomes the perimeter. Which of these is one of them?
options: Firewalls become the primary and sufficient control point
Trust stops being permanent — a user's standing can change mid-session rather than being fixed once network access is granted
VPN concentrators become the policy decision point
Device compliance becomes irrelevant to the access decision
questions.explain: One of the three architectural shifts is that trust must be re-earned continuously rather than assumed to persist once initially granted — which sets up Continuous Access Evaluation in the next lesson.
